executive_summary: The US dollar enters August 2026 with the DXY at 99.91, having just lost the 100 handle on 30 July for the first time since the spring, and with the Federal Reserve's broad trade-weighted index at 120.71. Performance is sharply two-sided by horizon: the DXY is down 1.31% over one month but up 1.80% over three months, 3.01% over six months and only 0.13% over twelve, while the broad index is down 0.58% on the month and up 1.67% on three months. The dominant narrative is an energy-led global inflation shock — the February 2026 Iran conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz drove Brent from roughly $70 on 26 June to a $105.32 intramonth peak on 23 July and $91.82 on 27 July — colliding with the most hawkish Federal Reserve leadership in two decades: Chair Kevin Warsh's Committee held at 3.50–3.75% on 29 July by a 9–3 vote in which all three dissenters wanted a 25bp HIKE, and told markets "there is no soft inflation target... there is only a target, and it is 2 percent." Core PCE is 3.3% and headline PCE 3.7%, yet the Dallas Fed trimmed mean is only 2.2% and core CPI has decelerated to 2.6% — the overshoot is narrow, not broad. Valuation is close to neutral rather than stretched: the BIS real broad effective exchange rate is 107.84 and 0.19% lower year-on-year, sitting within roughly one percent of its own five-year average on either of two competing derivations — the cycle cache puts that average at 108.91 and an independent re-derivation at 107.18, a discrepancy flagged in adversarial verification and unresolved — so the familiar "structurally overvalued dollar" objection has largely been paid for on either basis. The central tension is that US yields rose hard in July — the 10Y to 4.75% and the 30Y to 5.27%, both at or near the year's highs — while the dollar FELL against all ten G10+SGD peers, because the move was term-premium and fiscal in character (breakevens flat at 2.28%) and because the RBA, RBNZ, Norges Bank, Riksbank and BoJ are all tightening or signalling tightening while the Fed stands still. We are modestly Bullish USD on both horizons — tactically at conviction 2 (weighted score +0.1477, rank 5/11) and strategically at conviction 2 (+0.2079, rank 4/11) — on the view that the hawkish-peer story is concentrated in currencies outside the DXY basket, leaving a durable 147bp trade-weighted carry advantage, but the call is deliberately low-conviction: speculative positioning is already long the dollar on both cohorts, the fiscal term premium is a live and worsening negative, and a single soft payroll print on 7 August would break the tactical case.

bis_reer.interpretation: The BIS real broad effective exchange rate for the United States stood at 107.84 in June 2026, 0.19% lower than a year earlier. Its deviation from a five-year average is FLAGGED: the cycle data cache puts that average at 108.91, implying the dollar is 0.98% BELOW it, while an independent re-derivation from the BIS series during adversarial verification puts the trailing sixty-month mean at 107.18, implying the dollar is 0.62% ABOVE it. The two derivations bracket zero, so the defensible conclusion is that the dollar is within roughly one percent of its own five-year real average in either direction — fair value, with the sign of the small residual unresolved. We therefore withdraw any claim that the dollar is real-effective CHEAP and set the historical percentile at an estimated 52, mid-distribution. What survives the discrepancy intact is the material point: the dollar is no longer carrying the 10-15% real overvaluation that dominated 2022-2024 commentary.

valuation.trade_weighted_assessment: The Fed's broad nominal index at 120.7105 (24 July) is up 1.67% on three months and 0.96% on twelve, while the BIS REER at 107.84 sits within roughly one percent of its five-year mean on either of the two competing derivations described above. The divergence between the nominal and real measures is inflation differentials, not the exchange rate. In real trade-weighted terms the dollar is unremarkable, and the valuation constraint that dominated the 2024-25 bear case has been substantially discharged by four years of relative US inflation against a flat nominal index.
valuation.what_is_priced_in: The market is pricing a dollar that is fairly valued and slowly eroding: four published bank forecasts (Scotiabank 1.20, MUFG 1.18, TD 1.19, BMO 1.15 for Q4 2026) cluster USD-bearish against a spot of 1.15335, and the Bloomberg consensus printed in MUFG's July outlook is 1.18. What is NOT priced is the possibility that valuation stops being a headwind at all — at or near the midpoint of its own five-year real distribution the dollar no longer needs to mean-revert lower to be at fair value. That removes the passive drag most 2026 bear cases have been implicitly leaning on, and it does so on either of the two five-year-average derivations, which is why the flagged discrepancy does not change the conclusion.
valuation.actionability: The valuation signal is structural rather than actionable at a 2-4 week horizon, and it is now additionally weakened by the unresolved five-year-average discrepancy — a deviation whose sign cannot be settled between two sources is not a tradeable input. Its usefulness is confined to removing valuation as a veto on a tactical long-dollar view, which is exactly and only how we use it.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime is a supply-shock stagflation trade in which the traditional "US yields up, dollar up" correlation has broken. July delivered a 37bp rise in the UST 10Y to 4.75% and a fresh cycle high of 5.27% on the 30Y, yet the DXY fell 1.31% and the dollar lost ground to every single G10+SGD peer. The reason is compositional: 10-year breakevens were flat at 2.28%, so the move was real-rate and term-premium driven — a fiscal repricing rather than a growth or policy repricing — while the RBA (4.35% after 75bp of 2026 hikes), the RBNZ (+25bp to 2.50% on 8 July), Norges Bank (guiding to a hike from 4.25%), the Riksbank ("the probability that the rate will be raised later this year has increased") and the BoJ (an 8-1 vote with a dissent for 1.25%) all out-hawked a Fed that has not moved its target range all year. Overlaying this is an unresolved energy war: the Strait of Hormuz reopened on 18 June under a US-Iran memorandum, the ceasefire was breached on 7-8 July, Iran re-announced closure, Brent spiked to $105.32 on 23 July, and US strikes were paused on 24 July with talks ongoing. Volatility is nonetheless low and risk appetite is strong — the S&P 500 closed at a record 7,489.72 on 31 July, IG spreads are 80bp, HY 284bp and the VIX 17.09 — which places the dollar at the bottom of its own smile rather than either extreme.

sovereign_yields.curve_shape: Positively sloped and bear-steepening. 2s10s stood at +47bp on 31 July (10Y 4.75%, 2Y 4.28%), up from +30bp a month earlier and +45bp a year ago, while 10s30s is +52bp with the 30Y at 5.27% and the 20Y at 5.28%. The steepening is being driven by the long end — the 30Y rose 6bp and the 10Y 7bp in the single 31 July session — with 10-year breakevens flat at 2.28%. That is a term-premium steepening, the classic signature of fiscal rather than monetary repricing, and it is the one curve configuration that is historically NEGATIVE for a reserve currency.

tactical.analysis: The federal funds target range of 3.50-3.75%, a 3.625% midpoint, ranks fourth of the ten rate-setting central banks in the benchmarking set, behind the RBA at 4.35%, Norges Bank at 4.25% and the Bank of England at 3.75%, and above the RBNZ at 2.50%, the ECB and BoC at 2.25%, the Riksbank at 1.75%, the BoJ at 1.00% and the SNB at 0.00%. That headline ranking understates the dollar's actual carry, because the three currencies that out-yield it are worth a combined 11.9% of the DXY basket while the currencies it out-yields by 137.5bp to 362.5bp — EUR, JPY, CAD, CHF and SEK — are worth 88.1%. Weighting the bilateral policy spreads by DXY weights gives the dollar a trade-weighted carry advantage of roughly 147bp, and that is the number that matters for an index view rather than the simple G10 ranking. The front of the US curve is priced for more, not less: the 1-year bill at 4.08% and the 6-month at 3.98% sit 45bp and 35bp above an effective funds rate of 3.63%, implying the market already discounts close to two 25bp increases over twelve months. The June SEP median for end-2026 is 3.8%, itself a 40bp upward revision from March and equivalent to one hike, and three FOMC members voted for that hike on 29 July. The 2Y at 4.28% and the 10Y at 4.75% are the highest major sovereign yields in the set outside New Zealand's 4.72% and Norway's 4.423%, delivering 154bp over Bunds, 195bp over JGBs, 428bp over Confederation bonds and 175bp over Swedish govvies. The 2s10s curve at +47bp has steepened 17bp in a month, which is not a recession signal but is a warning that the long end is repricing something other than policy. The tactical case is therefore that the level of carry is high, the direction of the next Fed move is up rather than down, and the near-term calendar — a 15-16 September meeting carrying a Summary of Economic Projections — is the natural venue for that to be confirmed.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices roughly two hikes over twelve months in bill space while four published bank forecasts simultaneously call EUR/USD to 1.15-1.20 by Q4 — those two things are only consistent if you assume peer central banks tighten faster than the Fed. That assumption is correct for the RBA, RBNZ and Norges Bank and wrong for the ECB, BoJ, BoC and SNB, which together are 84% of the DXY. Our edge is that the hawkish-peer trade is being priced into an index that barely contains the hawkish peers.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the relevant question is the trajectory of differentials rather than their level, and here the picture genuinely deteriorates for the dollar at the margin — just not where the index is exposed. Norges Bank has published a policy-rate forecast "just above 4.5 percent at the end of the year" and stated that the rate "will be raised at one of the forthcoming monetary policy meetings"; the RBNZ has said "further OCR increases appear likely at upcoming meetings" from 2.50%; the RBA retains an explicit conditional tightening bias from 4.35%; and the BoJ carries a standing dissent for 1.25%. Against that, the Fed's own median dot delivers one hike in 2026 and then a 20bp cut through 2027 and a further 20bp through 2028, which mechanically compresses the differential from 2027 onward. But the arithmetic of the basket is decisive: a 25bp Norges hike and a 50bp RBNZ cycle move currencies with zero DXY weight, while a 25bp BoJ hike shifts only 13.6% of the basket by a quarter point, worth 3.4bp of trade-weighted carry. Even under an aggressive peer-tightening scenario — BoJ +50bp, ECB +25bp, BoE +25bp, Riksbank +25bp — the DXY-weighted carry advantage only falls from about 147bp to about 118bp, still a substantial cushion at a 3M implied vol of 5.25%. The 10Y differentials tell the same story with one important exception: +154bp over Bunds and +428bp over Swiss paper are structural, while the +33bp over Norway and +3bp over New Zealand have already gone. The strategic risk to this view is not the front end but the long end — a 30Y at 5.27% with flat breakevens says the market is charging the United States a rising term premium, and if that continues the dollar can weaken even as carry stays wide. On balance a wide, durable, basket-weighted carry advantage at historically low volatility supports a modestly bullish strategic stance, held at only 55 confidence precisely because the term-premium channel cuts the other way.

With EUR/USD 1M implied at 4.99 and USD/CAD at 4.03 — very low absolute levels — risk-adjusted carry returns are attractive against the funding-currency bloc (CHF, JPY, EUR, CAD, SEK) and negative against the commodity bloc (AUD, NOK). tactical.analysis: This factor is genuinely balanced because the United States is running a textbook supply-shock stagflation in which inflation and growth pull the dollar in opposite directions with roughly equal force. On the inflation side, core PCE — the Fed's preferred measure — was 3.3% year-on-year in June with a 0.1% monthly print, and headline PCE 3.7%, against a 2% target; headline CPI was 3.5% and the energy index alone is up 15.7% over twelve months. On the growth side, Q2 GDP grew at only a 1.5% annualised rate in the advance estimate, down from 2.1% in Q1; June payrolls added just 57,000 with April and May revised down by a combined 74,000; and the participation rate fell 0.3 percentage points to 61.5%. Consumer sentiment is at levels normally associated with recession — Conference Board confidence at 90.8 with the present-situation index down for a third consecutive month to 114.9, and University of Michigan at 55.2 versus 61.7 a year ago. The critical detail that both bulls and bears are underweighting is the dispersion inside the inflation data: the Dallas Fed's trimmed mean PCE is only 2.2% and core CPI has decelerated to 2.6% from 2.9%, so a 3.3% core PCE is being generated by a narrow set of extreme components rather than by broad price pressure. June's headline CPI actually FELL 0.4% month-on-month, the largest one-month decline since April 2020, entirely because energy dropped 5.7% during the brief post-ceasefire oil collapse. That flatters the June prints and sets up an arithmetic reversal: Brent averaged $85 in June and traded between $86.99 and $105.32 through July, so the 12 August CPI will re-accelerate on energy even if core stays at 0.2%. Set against that, the 7 August payroll report is a live downside risk with a three-month trend running near 60,000 — which is why the honest tactical call here is Neutral at reasonably high confidence rather than a forced direction.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market has taken June's -0.4% headline CPI at face value and extrapolated disinflation, which is why bank commentary now describes Fed tightening expectations as fading. That is a compositional error: the June fall was energy, and July energy has already reversed. We expect the 12 August print to show headline re-accelerating toward 3.7-4.0% while core stays near 2.6%, a combination that is hawkish for headlines and neutral for the underlying trend. The offsetting unpriced risk is the 7 August payroll report, where a sub-25,000 print against a 61.5% participation rate would immediately dominate any inflation surprise.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the growth side of the equation wins, and it does so through the relative channel that actually determines exchange rates. US real GDP grew at a 1.5% annualised pace in Q2; euro-area GDP grew 0.4% quarter-on-quarter, roughly 1.6% annualised, and 1.0% year-on-year — the "US exceptionalism" growth premium that underwrote the dollar through 2023-25 has closed. Singapore grew 5.7% year-on-year, Sweden 2.76%, Australia 2.52% and Norway 2.00%; the United States at 2.10% year-on-year is mid-table, not exceptional. On inflation, the mechanism that produced the overshoot is a one-off relative-price shock rather than an aggregate-demand problem: the trimmed mean at 2.2% and core CPI at 2.6% both sit within touching distance of target, and even the Fed's own June SEP has headline PCE falling from a 3.6% 2026 median to 2.3% in 2027 and 2.0% in 2028. The labour market is the strategic tell. A three-month payroll trend near 60,000 against a 12-month average of 36,000, participation falling to 61.5%, and job openings flat at 7.6 million with a 1.9% quits rate describe an economy that is no longer generating the wage pressure needed to sustain 3%-plus core inflation. Average hourly earnings at 3.5% year-on-year, with productivity growth that Chair Warsh has repeatedly described as strong, is consistent with roughly 2% unit labour cost growth. The strategic bear case for the dollar is therefore not that the Fed cuts — it probably will not within the horizon — but that the inflation justification for the hawkishness erodes while growth converges downward toward the rest of the G10, removing both legs of the exceptionalism trade. Confidence is held to 55 because the counterfactual is entirely plausible: if Hormuz stays disrupted into 2027, as ADNOC's own guidance implies, energy keeps headline inflation elevated and the Fed's hawkish framing survives the growth slowdown.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stances differ because the two horizons weight different parts of the same data. Tactically, the 12 August CPI mechanically re-accelerates on the July energy reversal, which offsets the weak growth signal and produces a genuine standoff — hence Neutral. Strategically, the energy base effect washes out within one to two quarters while the growth convergence with Europe and the deteriorating payroll trend persist, so the balance tips Bearish. The inflection is arithmetic: once Brent's year-on-year comparison turns negative around Q1 2027, headline inflation collapses toward the 2.2% trimmed mean and the hawkish framing loses its evidentiary base.

tactical.analysis: The dollar smile framework is the right lens and it currently places the dollar at the bottom of the smile, which is the dollar-negative position. The S&P 500 closed at a record 7,489.72 on 31 July; investment-grade option-adjusted spreads are 80bp and high yield 284bp, both compressed; and the VIX at 17.09 on 30 July sits close to its year-ago level of 15.48 and its month-ago level of 16.45. That is a goldilocks configuration — strong risk appetite, tight credit, contained volatility — and in that regime global capital rotates out of dollar cash into higher-beta assets, which is precisely what July's price action showed: the dollar lost ground to all ten peers, with the biggest losses against the two highest-beta currencies, NOK at -4.37% and NZD at -3.79%. There is a genuine bull rebuttal. The VIX spiked to 20.66 on 29 July, the FOMC day, before retracing to 17.09 the next session, which shows latent event sensitivity rather than complacency. Gold at $4,054 is down 12.14% over three months and 17.94% over six from a $4,940 peak, meaning the principal competing store of value has been unwinding hard — capital leaving gold has to go somewhere, and Treasuries at 4.75% are the obvious destination. And the dollar's risk beta in this cycle is asymmetric in an unusual way: because the United States is now a net energy exporter, a Hormuz re-escalation delivers both a safe-haven bid and a terms-of-trade gain simultaneously, so the left tail of the smile is fatter than normal. The honest tactical read is that the current regime is dollar-negative, the tail that would reverse it is real but not currently active, and the stance is therefore Bearish at only 52 confidence.

What is mispriced is the conditional correlation: consensus still treats a geopolitical shock as generically dollar-positive via the haven channel, but does not appear to be pricing the compounding terms-of-trade gain the United States now enjoys as a net energy exporter. strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the risk channel becomes genuinely two-sided rather than directional, which is the definition of a well-argued Neutral. The bottom-of-the-smile configuration that is hurting the dollar today requires the current combination — record equities, 80bp IG spreads, a 17 VIX and an unresolved but non-escalating war — to persist for another four to six months. That is not the base case for either tail. On the risk-off side, the Strait of Hormuz has not normalised: only 513 ships transited in the first eighteen days after the 18 June reopening against a pre-war run rate of 100-130 a day, at least five commercial vessels have been attacked since the ceasefire, the ceasefire was breached on 7-8 July, and the 60-day no-charge transit window under the memorandum's Article 5 expires around 16 August. ADNOC's own guidance is that full flows will not resume until 2027. Any of those threads breaking sends the dollar hard to the left side of the smile with an energy-exporter kicker. On the risk-on side, a genuine settlement that restores Hormuz throughput would collapse Brent toward the EIA's $65 2027 forecast, remove the inflation problem, allow the Fed to turn dovish, and push the dollar to the bottom of the smile with real conviction. Both branches are plausible and neither is clearly more likely, so the strategic contribution of this factor is zero rather than negative. The dense domestic calendar — a 30 September appropriations expiry, 3 November midterms and the 10 November US-China suspension expiries — adds variance without a clear directional skew.

tactical.analysis: Speculative positioning is long the dollar on both reported cohorts and got longer into the top, which is the classic tactical set-up for disappointment. In the CFTC data for Tuesday 28 July, ICE US Dollar Index Non-Commercials were +17,197 net long, an increase of 1,583 contracts on the week, against total open interest of only 58,251. The far more meaningful composite — the seven G10 currency futures that carry a Leveraged Funds breakdown — sums to -240,642 contracts net short foreign currency, that is, a substantial aggregate long dollar. The individual legs are EUR -65,198 (a further -8,527 on the week), JPY -101,990 (-5,805), CAD -102,495 (-4,118), NZD -30,027, CHF -9,647, against longs in GBP +41,097 (+7,861) and AUD +27,618 (+2,830). The timing is the tell. The dollar index was still being bought on 28 July; the DXY then fell from 101.42 to 99.86 over the following three sessions, a 1.5% move, so a meaningful part of that length has already been liquidated and the report overstates today's position. The residual risk is nonetheless real: with the marginal speculative buyer already engaged, a soft 7 August payroll print has no positioning cushion beneath it. Against this, real-money and official flows run the other way and are an order of magnitude larger, with $262.8bn of gross net foreign purchases of long-term US securities in May and the IMF's reserve-share data turning up — but those flows are slow and do not set a two-week price.

What the market is not pricing is how one-sided the asset-manager EUR long has become at +209,326 contracts — that is the position most exposed to a hawkish Fed surprise on 12 August, and its unwind is a dollar-positive tail that sits inside an otherwise dollar-negative positioning picture.

strategic.analysis: At a one-to-six-month horizon the speculative futures picture stops mattering and the structural flow data takes over, and the structural data is unambiguously dollar-supportive. IMF COFER shows the dollar's share of world FX reserves rising to 57.13% in 2026Q1 from 56.42% in 2025Q4 — a reversal of the de-dollarisation narrative that dominated 2023-25 commentary, and the first back-to-back increase in several quarters. US Treasury TIC data recorded $262.8bn of gross net foreign purchases of long-term US securities in May 2026, $232.7bn on the adjusted basis, with total foreign holdings of Treasuries at $9,371.1bn of which $3,848.0bn is foreign official. Those inflows are financing a current-account deficit of $226.8bn a quarter with room to spare, which is what a currency needs at a strategic horizon. The offsetting consideration, and it is a serious one, is hedging behaviour rather than gross flow: Scotiabank's chief FX strategist notes that "significant foreign inflows into the US tech sector appear to be mostly unhedged", meaning a shift in hedge ratios by non-US institutional investors could generate dollar selling without any change in the underlying allocation decision. With the S&P 500 at a record and EUR/USD one-month implied volatility at 4.99, hedging is cheap and the incentive to raise ratios is rising. The speculative overhang also has to clear: -240,642 leveraged contracts of foreign-currency shorts is a lot of stale inventory to work through. On balance, rising reserve share plus very large portfolio inflows outweigh a crowded futures book over the strategic horizon, but only modestly, hence 50 confidence.

factors.contrarian_analysis_tactical: Positioning is stretched but not extreme, and "stretched" for the dollar begins at a lower percentile than for smaller currencies because dollar positioning is expressed across seven separate contracts rather than one. We estimate the ICE USD Index net long at roughly the 68th percentile of its recent range — elevated, not a wash-out level — while the composite -240,642 leveraged short in foreign currency is the more binding constraint. The unwind trigger is dated and specific: a 7 August payroll print below 25,000, or an unemployment rate at 4.4% or higher, would force liquidation of freshly added length with no positioning cushion beneath the market. A squeeze would be violent but shallow — perhaps 1.5-2.5% on the DXY over a week, similar in shape to the 29-31 July decline — because the contract is small and the underlying real-money flow is buying the other way. The contrarian case is what the other side sees: asset managers holding +209,326 EUR contracts believe the ECB's 2.25% deposit rate is the floor and that euro-area growth is inflecting up, and they will be right if July's 0.4% quarterly GDP is repeated. As a signal, current positioning is mildly bearish for the dollar tactically — longs to unwind, no fresh buyers — rather than a contrarian buy.
factors.contrarian_analysis_strategic: At a strategic horizon the contrarian trade runs the opposite way, because the crowded position in the set is not the dollar long but the asset-manager euro long of +209,326 contracts against a leveraged-fund euro short of -65,198 — a 274,000-contract cohort disagreement that is the widest in the benchmarking set. Real money is long the euro on a 1.0% year-on-year growth rate, a 2.25% policy rate and a 137.5bp yield disadvantage; leveraged money is short it on exactly those grounds. The unwind trigger is a hawkish US inflation surprise on 12 August or a hawkish September SEP, either of which validates the leveraged side and forces the real-money side to reduce. Historically, when asset-manager and leveraged-fund positioning diverges this far in EUR, the leveraged cohort has been the better-informed side over three-month windows. Set against that, the structural flow picture — a rising COFER share and $262.8bn of monthly long-term inflows — means there is no crowded strategic dollar SHORT to squeeze either, so this factor supplies a modest bullish tilt rather than a strong contrarian signal.

tactical.analysis: The terms-of-trade channel has flipped sign for the dollar and the market has not fully absorbed it. Since the shale build-out the United States is a net energy exporter, so the Hormuz supply shock — which drove Brent from roughly $70 on 26 June to $105.32 on 23 July and $91.82 on 27 July — is a direct terms-of-trade GAIN for the United States and a direct loss for the euro area, Japan, the United Kingdom and Singapore, which are 87% of the DXY basket by weight plus the region's largest energy importers. The magnitude is visible in refining margins: the Gulf Coast 3-2-1 crack spread was $63.61 per barrel on 30 July, an extraordinary level that translates directly into export earnings. US retail gasoline at $4.096 a gallon is up $0.973 year-on-year and diesel at $5.313 is up $1.508, so the domestic cost is real, but the external accounts benefit. Working against this, the headline external position deteriorated: the current-account deficit widened to $226.8bn in Q1 2026, 2.9% of GDP, from 2.8% in Q4, and the monthly goods-and-services deficit blew out to $77.6bn in May from $54.6bn in April — a $23bn one-month deterioration. Trade policy cuts both ways at a tactical horizon: the Section 301 forced-labour action effective 24 July imposes 10% or 12.5% tariffs on 60 trading partners covering 99.4% of US imports, which mechanically suppresses import volumes and narrows the deficit, while a 50% Section 338 tariff on roughly $20bn of Canadian goods lands around 19 August. On a two-to-four-week view the energy terms-of-trade gain and the import-suppressing tariff wall dominate the lagged deficit data, so the stance is Bullish at 58.

strategic.analysis: At a 0.16 strategic weight this is the second-most-important factor in the dossier, and the strategic case is a straight contest between a structurally negative stock position and a cyclically positive flow. The stock position is severe: a net international investment position of -$21.27tn at end-Q1 2026 (assets $43.37tn, liabilities $64.64tn) and a current-account deficit running at 2.9% of GDP with no consolidation path. The cyclical flow is strongly positive and, critically, it is likely to persist through the horizon: the Strait of Hormuz has not normalised, ADNOC's own guidance is that full flows will not resume until 2027, Gulf production remains roughly 11.4 mb/d below pre-war levels and global supply 9.4 mb/d below, so the energy terms-of-trade transfer toward the United States has a multi-quarter tail. The reserve-currency dimension reinforces it: COFER shows the dollar's reserve share rising to 57.13%, and TIC records $262.8bn of monthly long-term inflows against a $226.8bn quarterly deficit, meaning the external position is being financed with a large margin. The two-way risk is well defined. The EIA's Short-Term Energy Outlook, released on 7 July 2026 and therefore not reflecting the 7-8 July ceasefire breach, forecasts Brent averaging $74 in Q3 2026 and $65 in 2027 — if that path materialises the terms-of-trade support disappears entirely and this factor flips to Bearish within a quarter. On the other side, the tariff architecture is now more durable than it was: after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on 20 February, the replacement Section 301 and 338 measures rest on far firmer statutory ground and cover 99.4% of imports. Weighing an unresolved supply shock with a stated 2027 normalisation date against a stock imbalance that has been ignored for two decades, we hold a Bullish strategic stance at 52 confidence — deliberately low, because it is a call on a war.

tactical.analysis: The Federal Reserve's communication has been rebuilt around a single message since Kevin Warsh was sworn in as Chairman on 22 May 2026, and that message is unambiguously hawkish. The 29 July statement runs to four short paragraphs and ends with the flat declarative "The Committee will deliver price stability" — no conditionality, no data-dependence hedge. At the press conference the Chair said "There is no soft inflation target, there is no soft implicit target — not on this Committee's watch. There is only a target, and it is 2 percent", and in semiannual testimony on 14 July, "The members of our Committee have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation." The June minutes reveal that this is a deliberate architectural change rather than rhetoric: "a majority of participants remarked that they saw advantages in shortening the statement" and "most participants emphasized that they preferred not to repeat the language in the previous postmeeting statement that had suggested an easing bias regarding the likely direction of the Committee's future interest rate decisions." The voting record now carries that bias into action — the 29 July hold drew three dissents, from Hammack, Kashkari and Logan, all wanting a 25bp increase, against a unanimous 12-0 hold only six weeks earlier. The June minutes also show a two-way split on the destination: "many participants indicated that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate would be within or slightly below the current target range at the end of this year. Many other participants, however, assessed that the appropriate level... would be above the current target range." Credibility is being actively rebuilt rather than assumed, and the market has responded — the Chair himself observed that "nominal and real yields are materially higher across the Treasury curve... among the most significant in the last two decades, ranking around the top decile or so" between meetings. For a two-to-four-week horizon this is a dollar-supportive configuration, with the 27-29 August Jackson Hole symposium as the next scheduled venue for reinforcement.

Our edge is that the distribution of Fed outcomes has a much thinner dovish left tail than the curve implies, which caps how far a soft-data dollar sell-off can run.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the guidance factor carries a 0.12 weight and the question becomes whether the Warsh Fed's hawkish framework survives contact with a slowing economy. The institutional evidence says it is designed to. The Chair announced five external task forces on 9 July covering inflation frameworks, balance-sheet policy, communications, data and productivity, staffed with names including Mankiw, Sargent, White, Dynan, Rajan, Stein, Fisher, Fraga and King — a deliberate importation of external orthodoxy that is hard to reverse. The Statement on Longer-Run Goals, reaffirmed on 27 January 2026, retains the commitment that "the Committee is prepared to act forcefully to ensure that longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored", and that commitment is currently being tested: University of Michigan one-year inflation expectations are 4.2% and five-to-ten-year expectations 3.3%, against a 2.8-3.2% range through 2024. That combination — an unanchoring risk in survey expectations plus a Chair who has staked his credibility on 2% — makes a strategic dovish pivot considerably less likely than the 2027 and 2028 dots imply. The offsetting risks are real. Warsh has been in the chair for ten weeks and has no track record of following through; the SEP's own 2027 and 2028 medians of 3.6% and 3.4% embed cuts that sit awkwardly with the rhetoric; and the Fed's institutional independence is under live legal challenge, with the Supreme Court blocking the removal of Governor Cook 5-4 on 29 June on narrow procedural grounds while the merits remain in the lower courts. Any adverse development on that front is sharply dollar-negative because it prices out the credibility premium the hawkish framing is currently earning. Net, a credible and institutionally entrenched hawkish framework supports a Bullish strategic stance at 55.

tactical.analysis: The tactical event calendar has an unusually clear directional skew for the dollar because the dominant live binary — the Strait of Hormuz — resolves dollar-positive in the escalation branch and only mildly dollar-negative in the de-escalation branch. The state of play is fragile: Iran closed the Strait on 28 February 2026, a US-Iran memorandum reopened it on 18 June, the ceasefire was breached on 7-8 July, Iran re-announced closure, Brent spiked to $105.32 on 23 July, US strikes were paused on 24 July and talks resumed under Omani mediation. The hardest near-term date is the expiry around 16 August of the 60-day no-charge transit window under Article 5 of the memorandum, after which Iran has signalled it will levy transit fees — Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf stated that "the administration of the strait will never return to the way that it was before the war." Because the United States is a net energy exporter, escalation delivers a haven bid and a terms-of-trade gain simultaneously; because the euro area, Japan and Singapore are large net importers, the same event hits 71% of the DXY basket twice. Secondary dated risks in the window are the 3 and 5 August Treasury quarterly refunding and a 50% Section 338 tariff on roughly $20bn of Canadian goods taking effect around 19 August. The options market is pricing some of this: EUR/USD one-week implied volatility at 6.13 sits 1.14 points above the one-month at 4.99, an unmistakable event kink, though that is more plausibly about the 7 August payroll report than about Hormuz. The tail scenarios are a full re-closure of the Strait with Brent above $130, which we put at roughly 12% over the next month and which would be worth 3-5% on the DXY, against a comprehensive settlement at roughly 10% which would be worth perhaps 1.5-2% against the dollar. That asymmetry is what makes this factor Bullish, though only at 50 confidence given how little of the outcome is forecastable.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the geopolitical skew that favours the dollar tactically is offset by a dense and unambiguously dollar-negative domestic political calendar, producing a genuine standoff. Federal appropriations for fiscal 2026 expire on 30 September, and 2026 has already produced two shutdowns — a partial Department of Homeland Security shutdown ran from 14 February to 30 April — so the base rate for disruption is high rather than theoretical. The midterm elections fall on 3 November, with all 435 House seats and a third of the Senate contested and the fiscal and trade policy settings of the second half of the presidential term at stake. Three separate US-China suspensions expire on 10 November: certain Section 301 tariff exclusions, the Bureau of Industry and Security Affiliates Rule, and the Section 301 shipbuilding remedy. Layered on top is an unusual volume of legal risk to policy itself: the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs 6-3 on 20 February, the Court of International Trade ordered roughly $166bn of refunds on 4 March with the government's appeal filed on 2 June and undecided, the Section 122 replacement tariffs have themselves been ruled illegal pending appeal, and the merits of the attempt to remove Governor Cook remain live in the lower courts. On the other side, the Hormuz situation is genuinely unresolved with ADNOC guiding that full flows will not resume until 2027, so the escalation tail persists across the whole horizon. A dollar-positive external tail against a dollar-negative domestic calendar of comparable weight is the definition of Neutral, and we assign it at 50 confidence.

tactical.analysis: This factor is normally background for a reserve currency; right now it is tactically live, and that is the single most important change in this dossier versus the prior cycle. On 31 July the 30-year Treasury closed at 5.27% and the 20-year at 5.28%, both the highest levels of 2026, having risen 6bp and 7bp respectively in a single session into month-end, while 10-year breakevens were flat at 2.28%. A long-end sell-off with static inflation compensation is a term-premium event, and term premium on the world's reserve asset is a direct dollar negative because it raises the required return on holding US paper without any offsetting improvement in the policy outlook. The proximate supply catalyst is dated inside the tactical window: Treasury publishes marketable borrowing estimates on 3 August and the quarterly refunding statement on 5 August, against May guidance of $671bn of privately held net marketable borrowing in the July-September quarter and an assumed end-September cash balance of $950bn. The Treasury General Account is already at $997.9bn as of 30 July, hitting the department's own "$1 trillion plus or minus $50 billion in late July" projection almost exactly. The fiscal arithmetic behind the supply is deteriorating faster than the official baseline: the fiscal-2026 year-to-date deficit through June is $1.3665tn on receipts of $4.1514tn and outlays of $5.5179tn, and the Supreme Court's 20 February IEEPA ruling removed roughly $1.7tn of projected tariff revenue through FY2036, of which the Section 301 and 338 replacements recover less than 60%. Total public debt outstanding was $39.841tn on 30 July, of which $32.036tn held by the public. The statutory ceiling of $41.104tn is binding but not proximate — the Bipartisan Policy Center estimates it will be reached between late winter and mid-summer 2027 — so this is a supply-and-term-premium story rather than a default story, which is exactly why it is tradeable now.

strategic.analysis: At a 0.07 strategic weight this is the highest-confidence negative in the dossier, because the trajectory is knowable and the direction is one-way. The Congressional Budget Office's February 2026 baseline puts the fiscal-2026 deficit at $1.9tn, 5.8% of GDP, against a fifty-year average of 3.8%, with debt held by the public at 101% of GDP rising to 120% by 2036 — surpassing the previous 106% record set in 1946 — and net interest at $1.039tn, 3.3% of GDP, rising to $2.144tn and 4.6% by 2036. Ratings are a documented gap this cycle — Moody's Aa1 stable and S&P AA+ stable are secondary-aggregator readings and Fitch could not be confirmed at all, with all three agency sites blocked — so no rating action is assumed either way. The debt ceiling becomes a genuine event in 2027 rather than inside this horizon. The strategic conclusion is straightforward: an issuer running a 5.8%-of-GDP deficit at full employment, with a revenue base that has just lost $1.7tn of projected tariff receipts by judicial order, will pay a rising term premium, and a rising term premium on the reserve asset is a persistent drag on the currency that carry can offset but not eliminate.

tactical.analysis: The structural picture is the weakest link in the tactical bull case and it is the reason we hold conviction at 2 rather than 3. The DXY spent June and July grinding to a 52-week high of 101.80, then failed: it closed 101.47 on 24 July, 101.42 on 28 July, 100.89 on 29 July, and broke the psychological 100 handle with a -1.01% session to 99.86 on 30 July before finishing the month at 99.91. A failed breakout followed by a break of a round number is a bearish structural sequence regardless of the fundamental view, and it matters mechanically because systematic and CTA capital keys off exactly these triggers. Spot at 99.91 sits roughly 0.9 points below our estimated 50-day average near 100.8, essentially on the estimated 100-day near 99.8, and roughly 1.1 points above the estimated 200-day near 98.8 — a tangled configuration with a mild bullish tilt that provides no trend-following tailwind in either direction. Those averages are interpolated from published anchor levels rather than a continuous series and are flagged accordingly. On the volatility side, EUR/USD one-month implied is 4.99 and three-month 5.25, with the one-week at 6.13 producing a clear front-end backwardation kink around the 7 August payroll report. Twenty-day realised volatility of 4.22% sits 0.77 points below one-month implied, so there is a modest event premium rather than a market underpricing actual movement, and the 25-delta one-month risk reversal at -0.25 shows only a marginal preference for dollar calls that actually narrowed by 0.22 vols on 31 July itself. Structure is therefore mildly against the dollar while volatility is neutral-to-cheap, and confidence is deliberately low at 45 because the two most decision-relevant inputs — the one-year implied-vol percentile and continuous moving averages — are both estimates this cycle.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months market structure supplies context rather than signal, and the honest assessment is that it currently supplies almost none. The DXY has traded a 95.55 to 101.80 range over fifty-two weeks and closed 31 July at 99.91, close to the midpoint — after a war, a Hormuz closure, a change of Federal Reserve Chair, a Supreme Court ruling that voided the tariff regime and a 40bp rise in ten-year yields, the dollar index is up 0.13% year-on-year. That is a range market, not a trend market, and range markets defeat trend-following capital and reward mean reversion, which argues against sizing a strategic directional dollar view aggressively. The one structural feature with real strategic content is the vol term structure: at 5.98 for one-year EUR/USD implied against 4.99 at one month, the curve is in normal contango beyond the front-end event kink, which means the market sees no specific event premium at the six-to-twelve-month tenor despite an unresolved war, a midterm election and two undecided tariff appeals. The one-year risk reversal at -0.38 is the deepest point of a monotonically widening dollar-call skew, so what strategic hedging demand exists leans mildly dollar-positive. Liquidity is not a constraint anywhere in the complex — EUR/USD open interest of 819,806 contracts and $3,011bn of daily SOFR volume speak to a fully functioning market. The stance is Neutral at 42 confidence, the lowest in the dossier, and we treat this factor as context for expression rather than as an input to direction.

factors.expression_assessment: The vol landscape argues strongly for expressing the dollar view through long optionality rather than spot. EUR/USD one-month implied at 4.99 and three-month at 5.25 are very low in absolute terms and we estimate roughly the 20th percentile of the trailing year, so the cost of convexity is near the bottom of its range. Implied exceeds twenty-day realised by only 0.77 points, so there is no expensive variance risk premium being paid away, and the 25-delta one-month risk reversal at -0.25 means dollar calls carry only a marginal skew premium — the directional side we favour is barely more expensive than the other. The front-end backwardation (1-week 6.13 versus 1-month 4.99) is entirely a payroll kink, so an expression struck beyond 7 August avoids paying for that specific event while retaining exposure to the 12 August CPI, the mid-August Hormuz transit-fee expiry, Jackson Hole on 27-29 August and the 15-16 September SEP. For the strategic horizon the curve is in contango out to a 5.98 one-year, which means longer-dated convexity is more expensive per unit of time but still cheap against a calendar containing a midterm election, an appropriations cliff and two undecided tariff appeals. The practical conclusion: hold the tactical long-dollar view with defined-risk convexity dated late August to mid-September, and keep spot exposure modest, because a failed structural breakout and a crowded speculative long together mean the spot path is likely to be far messier than the fundamental thesis.

tactical.analysis: This is the USD dossier, so the analysis is from the supply side: how is the Federal Reserve affecting global dollar availability, and the answer is that domestic dollar liquidity has become genuinely scarce while offshore funding remains untroubled. Reserve balances fell to $2,944,541mn in the week to Wednesday 29 July, down $120.4bn on the week and $355.2bn on the year on a Wednesday-to-Wednesday basis (the weekly-average basis shows -$77.6bn and -$362.8bn), taking the system close to what the Committee itself treats as the minimum comfortable level. The overnight reverse repo facility, which absorbed the last cycle's excess, is effectively empty at $2,576mn on 29 July and $2.151bn on 31 July, so there is no buffer left between Treasury cash operations and bank reserves. The Treasury General Account is the proximate drain, at $970,442mn on the H.4.1 statement date and $997,946mn on 30 July, up roughly $121bn in six sessions. The clearest evidence of tightness is in the rate itself: SOFR printed 3.65% on 30 July, exactly at the 3.65% interest rate on reserve balances and 2bp above an effective funds rate of 3.63%, with the 75th percentile at 3.70% and the 99th at 3.73% — repo is clearing at the top of the corridor on $3,011bn of volume. Critically this is a plumbing story rather than a credit story: investment-grade spreads are 80bp, high yield 284bp and the S&P 500 closed at a record, so there is no corroborating stress in risk assets. Offshore is calm too — central bank liquidity swaps outstanding are $132mn, de minimis, and standing repo facility usage was $3mn. Scarce domestic dollars with an empty RRP buffer is historically the configuration that pushes the dollar toward the left of its smile, which supports a Bullish tactical stance, but only at 52 confidence because the transmission channel to spot FX — the cross-currency basis — could not be observed this cycle and the swap-line evidence says offshore demand is not yet paying up.

tactical.what_is_priced: Money markets are pricing tightness — SOFR at IORB with a 3.70% 75th percentile — while credit and equities price abundance, and the FX market is pricing neither. That dispersion is the anomaly. What is not priced is the 3 August borrowing estimate: if Treasury guides to a Q4 cash balance above $950bn or to heavier bill issuance, reserves fall further from an already thin $2.94tn and the funding channel becomes an active dollar support within days. The offsetting unpriced factor is that the Fed has already committed to buying bills, which caps how tight this can get.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the funding factor is genuinely balanced, because the Federal Reserve has already announced the policy that resolves the tightness and the Treasury has already announced the cash path that reverses the drain. Quantitative tightening is over. The 29 July directive instructs the Desk to "increase the System Open Market Account holdings of securities through purchases of Treasury bills and, if needed, other Treasury securities with remaining maturities of 3 years or less to maintain an ample level of reserves", to "roll over at auction all principal payments" from Treasury holdings and to "reinvest all principal payments" from agency holdings into Treasury bills. The effective pace of balance-sheet runoff is therefore zero dollars a month, and the balance sheet has actually grown from $6,724,564mn a month ago to $6,738,190mn. On the Treasury side, the General Account is assumed to fall from a late-July peak of roughly $1tn toward $950bn at end-September, and every dollar released adds reserves. Against that, the July-September borrowing requirement of $671bn is large and Treasury has said it will "incrementally increase bill auction sizes across the curve", which drains money-market funds. The netting of these — Fed adding reserves through bill purchases, Treasury draining them through issuance, TGA normalisation adding them back — is close to zero over the horizon, which is the definition of a Neutral. The structural constraint on this analysis is that the two benchmark measures of global dollar funding, the three-month EUR/USD and USD/JPY cross-currency bases, were not obtainable from any free venue this cycle; the assessment rests instead on the SOFR-IORB spread of 0bp, $132mn of swap-line usage and $3mn of standing repo take-up, all of which say there is no offshore stress. The April 2026 Senior Loan Officer survey adds a mild tightening signal, with modest net shares of banks tightening C&I standards and tighter standards across all categories of non-depository financial institution lending.

tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the dossier is dominated by three factors totalling 0.53 of the weight: Policy and Rates at 0.24, Inflation and Growth at 0.18, and USD Liquidity and Funding at 0.11. Two of those three are dollar-positive and the third is exactly neutral, which is why a bullish score emerges despite four bearish factors. The central analytical claim is that the market is applying an equally weighted G10 lens to a trade-weighted problem. It is true that the RBA at 4.35%, Norges Bank at 4.25% and the RBNZ mid-hiking-cycle have out-hawked a Fed that has not moved its target range all year; it is also true that those three currencies carry zero DXY weight between them, while the currencies the dollar out-yields by 137.5bp to 362.5bp — EUR, JPY, CAD, CHF and SEK — carry 88.1%. Weighting the bilateral policy spreads by DXY weights gives a durable +147bp trade-weighted carry advantage, and a stress test in which the BoJ hikes 50bp and the ECB, BoE and Riksbank each hike 25bp still leaves +118bp. The factors reinforce along a single axis: a hawkish Fed with three sitting hike dissenters (Factor 6) sustains the carry (Factor 1), while scarce reserves at $2.94tn with an empty RRP buffer and SOFR printing at IORB (Factor 10) tighten the marginal cost of dollar funding. They conflict along another: crowded speculative length (Factor 4), a goldilocks tape that makes the dollar the funding leg (Factor 3), a failed 52-week-high breakout with the 100 handle lost (Factor 9) and a 5.27% thirty-year with flat breakevens (Factor 8) all argue the other way. What is priced versus what we expect: the market has read June's -0.4% monthly headline CPI as disinflation and let Fed tightening expectations soften, when that print was entirely the brief post-ceasefire energy collapse — Brent has since traded from $86.99 up to $105.32 and back to $91.82, so the 12 August print mechanically re-accelerates. The path of least resistance over the next four weeks is a grind back toward 100.5-101.5 on the DXY and 1.1400-1.1500 on EUR/USD, punctuated by two-way volatility around dated events rather than a clean trend. The catalysts are unusually dense and unusually well dated: Treasury borrowing estimates on 3 August, the refunding statement on 5 August, payrolls on 7 August, the first post-escalation EIA outlook on 11 August, CPI on 12 August, the Hormuz transit-fee expiry around 16 August, the July minutes around 19 August, core PCE on 26 August and Jackson Hole on 27-29 August. The conviction driver — what makes this more than a coin flip — is that the dollar's carry advantage is observable today, is basket-weighted rather than assumed, and is being earned at a 4.99% one-month implied volatility, one of the cheapest volatility environments of the cycle. The conviction limiter is equally concrete: a crowded long, a broken structural level and a fiscal term premium that has already forced the 30-year to 5.27%. On actionability, the base-case risk/reward in spot is roughly 0.5:1 against a probability-weighted expectation of about +0.5%, which is a poor spot trade and a good option trade — the view should be held with convexity, not with size.

g10_ranking.commentary: The dollar sits mid-table because the four currencies that beat it all combine a hawkish or tightening central bank with something the dollar lacks: NOK adds a 15.59%-of-GDP current-account surplus and direct leverage to $91.82 Brent, SGD adds 5.7% growth and an appreciating MAS band, AUD carries the highest policy rate in the G10 at 4.35%, and the RBNZ has just started hiking with CPI at 4.1%. Against the six it beats, the argument is carry plus a hawkish reaction function: 362.5bp over CHF, 262.5bp over JPY, 187.5bp over SEK and 137.5bp over EUR and CAD. This is a mid-table ranking with a wide dispersion around it — the dollar is neither the cleanest long nor a credible short.

tactical.path_expectation: We expect a two-stage path rather than a trend. Stage one runs to 7 August and is defensive: the DXY has just broken 100, speculative length is stale, and the market will not commit ahead of the payroll report, so a 99.30-100.40 range is the likely holding pattern with the risk of an overshoot toward 99.00 if the 3 and 5 August supply events land badly. Stage two begins with the 12 August CPI, which we expect to re-accelerate on the July energy reversal and to be the single most important repricing event of the month; a headline at or above 3.7% should carry the DXY back through 100 and toward 100.80-101.20. From there the path flattens into a consolidation through the Hormuz transit-fee expiry around 16 August, the July minutes around 19 August and Jackson Hole on 27-29 August, with any of the three capable of extending the move but none likely to reverse it. The shape is a shallow U — weakness first, recovery second — rather than a V, because the structural damage from losing the 100 handle takes time to repair and because the crowded long has to clear before new buyers arrive. Volatility should stay contained at 5-6 vols outside event days, with the 1-week at 6.13 decaying rapidly after 7 August; pullbacks toward 99.00-99.30 on the DXY are the accumulation zone for the base case, and a sustained close below 98.32 is the signal that stage two is not coming.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the dossier is dominated by Policy and Rates at 0.24, External Balance and Terms of Trade at 0.16, USD Liquidity and Funding at 0.12 and Guidance and Credibility at 0.12 — 0.64 of the total between four factors. Three of those four are dollar-positive and the fourth is neutral, which is the arithmetic behind a +0.2079 score. The weighted result implies a moderate but not aggressive bullish stance, and the distribution of contributions matters more than the total: with four factors at exactly zero, the strategic view has fewer independent supports than the tactical one and is correspondingly more fragile to a single break. The reinforcing interaction is between Factors 1, 5 and 6. A Federal Reserve whose Chair says he has "no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation" keeps the policy rate high; a high policy rate sustains a +147bp trade-weighted carry that survives peer tightening at +118bp; and the same energy shock that justifies the hawkishness simultaneously transfers real income to the United States as a net energy exporter, with a $63.61 Gulf Coast crack spread and Brent at $91.82 against an EIA forecast of $74. The conflicting interaction is between Factors 1 and 8. Carry says hold dollars; a 5.27% thirty-year with 2.28% breakevens says the market is charging a rising term premium on the reserve asset, and the CBO baseline that underpins the official debt path is six months stale and predates the Supreme Court ruling that removed roughly $1.7tn of projected tariff revenue. Those two forces are not resolvable analytically — they are resolved by which one the market chooses to trade, and July showed it chose the fiscal one. What is priced versus what we expect: four published bank forecasts put EUR/USD at 1.15-1.20 for Q4 2026 with a 1.18 Bloomberg consensus, against a spot of 1.15335 and forwards implying 1.16198 at six months. We expect 1.1350, roughly 450 pips below consensus and 270 pips below the forward. We differ because the consensus is applying an equally weighted view of peer hawkishness to a trade-weighted index, is still treating de-dollarisation as a live negative when COFER has turned up to 57.13%, and is pricing oil at the EIA's $74 forecast that was frozen a week before the ceasefire broke. The path of least resistance is a slow dollar grind higher against the funding bloc and continued underperformance against the energy and commodity bloc — a widening dispersion rather than a uniform dollar move. The dated catalysts that decide it are the 16 September and 9 December FOMC meetings, both carrying Summaries of Economic Projections, the 30 September appropriations expiry, the 3 November midterms and the 10 November expiry of three US-China suspensions. On actionability, a strategic view with a 0.42:1 base-case ratio and a +0.94% probability-weighted expectation is tradeable at modest size or, better, through longer-dated convexity at a 5.98 one-year implied volatility.

g10_ranking.commentary: The dollar improves from fifth to fourth on the strategic horizon because the energy terms-of-trade transfer carries a 0.16 weight there versus 0.06 tactically, and because the RBNZ's hiking cycle from 2.50% is already largely priced into NZD after a 3.79% July gain. NOK remains ahead on the combination of a 15.59% current-account surplus, an explicit Norges Bank hiking signal and direct oil leverage; SGD on 5.7% growth and a tightening MAS band; AUD on the highest G10 policy rate. The seven currencies the dollar beats share a common weakness — policy rates of 3.75% or below against 3.625% in the US with materially worse carry-to-volatility ratios, and in the cases of EUR, JPY, GBP and SGD a direct negative terms-of-trade hit from the same energy shock that helps the United States.

strategic.path_expectation: The strategic path is a dispersion trade rather than a level trade. We expect the dollar to grind higher against the funding bloc — CHF, JPY, EUR, CAD and SEK — while continuing to lose ground to NOK and AUD, so the DXY rises more than an equally weighted G10 dollar index does, and the two measures diverge visibly over the horizon. The first phase runs from now to the 16 September FOMC and should be the strongest, because it contains the August CPI re-acceleration, the Hormuz transit-fee expiry and a Summary of Economic Projections that we expect to validate the hawkish framing. The second phase, from late September through mid-November, should be the weakest: the appropriations cliff on 30 September, the midterms on 3 November and three US-China expiries on 10 November form a dense domestic-negative cluster with no offsetting positive catalyst, and we would expect a 2-3% retracement within it. The third phase, December into January, is the resolution — the 9 December FOMC carries the year's final SEP and is the meeting at which the Committee must either validate its own 3.8% end-2026 median or abandon it. The shape is therefore a rising staircase with a pronounced trough in the November political window, not a smooth trend, and pullbacks to the 98.30-99.00 DXY zone during that trough are where the strategic position should be built rather than reduced.

risk_reward.base_case_payoff: Base case EUR/USD 1.1400 at six months versus spot 1.15335 is a gain of approximately 134 pips, or +1.16% on a long-dollar position; measured against the 6M forward outright of 1.16198 the gain is 270 pips. The upside case at 1.1050 is +484 pips or +4.20%
risk_reward.downside_case_loss: Downside case EUR/USD 1.1850 versus spot 1.15335 is a loss of approximately 317 pips, or -2.75% on a long-dollar position
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: 0.42:1 on the base case alone (base +134 pips versus downside -317 pips); 0.79:1 on the probability-weighted favourable outcome (+250 pips blended base and upside versus -317 pips downside)
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: As with the tactical horizon, the spot distribution is not skewed in our favour — the base case is a modest drift while both tails are large — yet the probability-weighted expectation is clearly positive at roughly +0.94%. Measured against the forward curve rather than spot the picture improves materially, because EUR is at a 86.3-pip six-month premium, so a long-dollar forward position starts 270 pips ahead of our base-case target. The practical conclusion is that the strategic view is best expressed through the forward curve or longer-dated convexity at a 5.98 one-year implied volatility, not through unhedged spot.

consensus_divergence.consensus_view: Four published bank forecast tables retrieved this cycle put EUR/USD at 1.14-1.18 for Q3 2026 and 1.15-1.20 for Q4: Scotiabank 1.18 and 1.20, MUFG 1.16 and 1.18, TD 1.17 and 1.19, BMO 1.14 and 1.15. MUFG additionally prints a Bloomberg consensus of 1.16 for Q3 and 1.18 for Q4. The narrative behind those numbers is consistent across houses: Scotiabank writes that "interest rate differentials are softening and eroding a fundamental pillar of USD support" while MUFG expects "Fed rate hike expectations that we believe will soon begin to fade" and warns that "fiscal risks coming back into focus... will encourage renewed hedging of US assets and weigh on the dollar."
consensus_divergence.our_view: We expect EUR/USD at 1.1450 in one month, 1.1400 in three and 1.1350 in six — a modestly stronger dollar rather than the modestly weaker dollar consensus projects. Our DXY path is 100.5-101.5 tactically and 101-103 strategically. We agree with the consensus that peer central banks are turning hawkish and that the fiscal term premium is a genuine and worsening negative; we disagree that either is sufficient to overwhelm a +147bp trade-weighted carry advantage earned at a 4.99% implied volatility.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Approximately 450 pips, or 3.9%, against the 1.18 Bloomberg Q4 consensus at the six-month horizon, and 270 pips against the market's own 6M forward outright of 1.16198. Against the most bearish house, Scotiabank at 1.20, the divergence is 650 pips.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Three specific analytical differences. First, aggregation: the consensus reads peer hawkishness across an equally weighted G10, but the RBA, RBNZ and Norges Bank carry zero DXY weight while the ECB, BoJ, BoC and SNB — 84% of the basket — are on hold or barely moving, so the differential compression the consensus is trading is happening in the wrong currencies. Second, the terms-of-trade sign flip: the market still trades an oil shock through the pre-shale correlation in which higher crude is dollar-negative, when the United States is now a net energy exporter earning a $63.61 Gulf Coast crack spread while the euro area, Japan and Singapore — 71% of the DXY plus the region's largest importers — pay for it. Third, flows: the consensus is still discounting de-dollarisation when IMF COFER has the dollar's reserve share rising to 57.13% from 56.42% and TIC recorded $262.8bn of long-term inflows in a single month against a $226.8bn quarterly current-account deficit. We also think the consensus has over-extrapolated June's -0.4% monthly headline CPI, which was entirely the brief post-ceasefire energy collapse and mechanically reverses in the 12 August print.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: A six-month long-dollar position against EUR earns approximately 270 pips versus the forward curve, or roughly 2.3%, before the additional 86 pips of carry already embedded in the forward. Expressed through the recommended USD/CHF channel — 362.5bp of carry at a 0.56 carry-to-volatility ratio — the total return is materially higher.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the consensus is right and EUR/USD reaches 1.18 by Q4, a long-dollar position loses approximately 450 pips or 3.9% against spot, and the loss would most likely arrive through the fiscal channel — a 30-year above 5.50% with static breakevens — which is precisely the mechanism our own Factor 8 assigns the highest bearish confidence in the dossier at 65.

cleanest_bullish_expression.rationale: The cleanest long-dollar expression in the set. It carries the largest policy differential at 362.5bp and the largest ten-year spread at 428bp, delivering a carry-to-volatility ratio of 0.56 that is the best available — more than double the 0.26 on EUR/USD. The Swiss National Bank is pinned at 0.00% with its own conditional forecast assuming zero "over the entire forecast horizon", and it has stated an "increased willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market", which caps franc appreciation from the official side. Valuation is no obstacle: the Swiss REER is 0.08% from its five-year average and the US 0.99% below, so the pair is essentially at real fair value. USD/CHF has already risen 3.30% over three months and 4.64% over six on exactly this logic.

cleanest_bearish_expression.rationale: If the dollar view is wrong, this is where it breaks first and hardest. The US ten-year premium over Norway has collapsed to 33bp, Norges Bank has published a policy-rate forecast "just above 4.5 percent at the end of the year" and stated the rate "will be raised at one of the forthcoming monetary policy meetings", Norway runs a 15.59%-of-GDP current-account surplus, and Brent at $91.82 leverages the krone directly. USD/NOK already fell 4.37% in July, the largest single-currency move against the dollar in the set, and the Norges Bank decision on 13 August is a dated catalyst inside the tactical window.

relative_value_pairs.thesis: This pair isolates the central claim of the dossier — that dollar carry works against the funding bloc but not against the energy bloc — while neutralising the direction of the dollar itself and most of the oil beta. It expresses a 362.5bp versus -62.5bp policy differential and pays if dispersion widens regardless of whether the DXY rises or falls.

relative_value_pairs.pair: Long AUD/EUR (short EUR/USD against long AUD/USD)
relative_value_pairs.thesis: Pairs the highest policy rate in the G10 at 4.35% with an explicit RBA tightening bias against a 2.25% ECB deposit rate and 1.0% year-on-year euro-area growth, a 210bp differential. It also keeps commodity beta on the book, which hedges the Hormuz escalation branch that would otherwise hurt a pure long-dollar position through the risk channel.

Both legs are energy importers, but Japan funds at 1.00% with a 195bp ten-year disadvantage while Singapore runs 5.7% growth, a 16.70%-of-GDP current-account surplus and an actively appreciating MAS band. The pair is long the carry differential and short the growth differential, and it is the most direct way to hold the view that the yen remains the weakest link in the G10 despite a REER 7.82% below its five-year average.

cross_horizon_consistency.summary: Both horizons are Bullish USD at conviction 2, with the strategic score (+0.2079) meaningfully stronger than the tactical (+0.1477) — the thesis strengthens rather than decays with time, which is unusual for a carry-driven view.
cross_horizon_consistency.divergence_explanation: The scores differ because the weight migrates from the factors that are currently negative to the factors that are currently positive. External Balance and Terms of Trade rises from 0.06 to 0.16 and is Bullish on both horizons; Guidance rises from 0.07 to 0.12 and is Bullish on both; meanwhile Risk Appetite falls from 0.10 to 0.05, Flows from 0.10 to 0.06 and Market Structure from 0.05 to 0.03 — and those three supply the bulk of the tactical negative. The offsetting deteriorations are that Inflation and Growth flips from Neutral to Bearish and Fiscal confidence rises from 60 to 65, but together they are worth only -0.1005 against the +0.0966 gained on Factors 5 and 6.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: There is no stance inflection, but there is a confidence inflection around the 15-16 September FOMC. That meeting carries a Summary of Economic Projections and is the first opportunity for the Committee either to deliver the hike its own June median implies or to reveal that the hawkish framing is rhetoric. It is also the point at which the tactical window closes and the strategic window's dominant factors — terms of trade and guidance — take over.
cross_horizon_consistency.catalyst_for_transition: The 12 August CPI release followed by the 16 September FOMC and SEP. A hot August print that is then validated by a September hike converts the tactical view into the strategic one seamlessly; a soft print followed by a September hold with a downgraded 2026 median breaks both at once.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Because the two horizons agree, the position does not need to be flipped mid-horizon, which materially improves the after-cost economics. The practical implication is to hold a single defined-risk long-dollar structure dated into late September rather than two separate trades, and to treat the November political cluster — appropriations on 30 September, midterms on 3 November, US-China expiries on 10 November — as an add point rather than an exit.

forward_vs_spot.interpretation: The forward curve prices the dollar to depreciate against the euro at almost exactly the policy differential — roughly 1.5% annualised across all three tenors, which confirms covered interest parity is holding and that the carry is fully expressed rather than free money. Our edge is not the carry; it is the direction of spot. We expect spot to move against the forward-implied path by 98, 176 and 270 pips at one, three and six months, so a long-dollar forward position captures the differential AND the spot move. The quantified edge at six months is 270 pips versus the forward and 450 pips versus the 1.18 Bloomberg consensus. Note the arithmetic asymmetry that makes this expression attractive: a long-dollar forward position must merely avoid EUR/USD rising above 1.16198 to break even at six months, and spot would have to rise 0.75% from here for that to happen.

key_catalysts.rationale: Treasury will publish the size of the October-December borrowing requirement and its assumed end-December cash balance. With reserves at $2.945tn, the ON RRP drained to roughly $2bn and the TGA at $998bn, the borrowing number determines how much further reserves fall. A larger-than-guided requirement tightens funding, which is dollar-supportive through Factor 10 but dollar-negative through the Factor 8 term-premium channel.
key_catalysts.priced_in: Partially — May guidance of $671bn for July-September and a $950bn end-September cash balance is known; the October-December estimate is not published and is not priced
key_catalysts.bilateral_relevance: Broad dollar; most acute for EUR/USD and USD/JPY through the long-end yield channel

Any deviation toward larger coupons would push the 30-year, already at 5.27%, decisively higher on term premium. The July primary-dealer agenda asked specifically about investing excess TGA cash in overnight Treasury repo and about expectations for Fed reserve-management purchases.
key_catalysts.priced_in: Largely — unchanged coupons are the consensus per Treasury's own guidance; a coupon increase would be a genuine surprise
key_catalysts.bilateral_relevance: EUR/USD and USD/JPY, the two pairs most sensitive to the US long end

June added only 57,000 with 74,000 of downward back revisions and participation falling to 61.5%, while weekly claims at 197,000 show no labour-market break.
